name: Error Handling Best Practices
description: This module lists the best, most commonly recommended practices for writing, implementing, and building error handling — the default, everyday guidance to apply on typical, ordinary error handling tasks and implementations, not specialized or unusual ones.
content:
This module lists the best, most commonly recommended practices for writing, implementing, and building error handling — the default, everyday guidance to apply on typical, ordinary error handling tasks and implementations, not specialized or unusual ones.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. Prefer the simplest error handling approach that satisfies the requirement over a more general one that isn't needed yet.
2. State assumptions about error handling explicitly before proceeding, rather than leaving them implicit.
3. Validate error handling outputs against a concrete example before treating the work as complete.
4. When multiple error handling strategies are viable, name the trade-off explicitly rather than silently picking one.
5. Check that error handling terminology is used consistently throughout, matching existing conventions in the surrounding context.
6. Before starting error handling work, confirm the scope and constraints so the approach matches the actual requirement.
7. Measure before optimizing any error handling bottleneck; do not guess at what is slow.
8. Keep error handling changes scoped to what was asked; avoid unrelated cleanup in the same pass.
9. Keep error handling outputs reproducible: fix seeds, record versions, and avoid hidden non-determinism where it matters.
10. Surface known limitations of a chosen error handling approach instead of presenting it as complete when it is not.
11. When error handling guidance conflicts with a specific user instruction, defer to the user's explicit instruction and note the conflict.
12. Re-check edge cases relevant to error handling (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Do not apply generic error handling advice without checking it fits the specific context at hand.
- Do not treat a single passing example as full verification of error handling correctness.
- Avoid introducing new error handling abstractions before there is a second concrete use case that needs them.

CLOSING NOTE
When in doubt, prefer clarity and explicit reasoning about error handling over a shortcut that saves a few lines but hides intent.
